title: New Cyclone Approaches Nepal - Explorersweb »
description: New Cyclone Approaches Nepal  Explorersweb »
publisher.title: Explorersweb »
full_article:
For the second time in just over a month, a violent storm is approaching Nepal and threatening two meters of fresh snow on already overloaded mountains. This new setback comes at the height of the trekking season and also affects several climbing teams, including those engaged in alpine-style expeditions in remote areas.

The first storm hit Nepal toward the end of September and abruptly ended the climbing season on Manaslu. Worst of all, it caused an avalanche that killed 16 Base Camp staff on Himlung. The mountain remained open to commercial expeditions despite the accident, and several guided teams are currently launching their summit pushes.

Manaslu Base Camp tents buried under the snow after the September storm in Nepal. Photo: Shiddi Ghising

Forecast

A low-pressure front that formed in the Bay of Bengal has now developed into a deep depression and will turn into a full cyclone tomorrow. It is expected to hit Nepal on Wednesday or Thursday through the end of the week.

The Nepal National Mountain Guides Association, in association with Senior Meteorologist Krishna Bhakta Manandhar, has put out a detailed forecast. They note that clouds spreading out from this system will hit Nepal’s mountains on October 28, especially above 6,500-7,000m in the eastern part of Nepal, including the Khumbu and Kanchenjunga regions. This will spread over the next two days, causing heavy rains throughout Nepal and snow at higher altitudes.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Warnings

Authorities and local media have urged trekkers and climbers to modify their plans and avoid river areas and high passes. The main concern is for those currently in remote areas without InReach, Starlink, or satphones.

Trekkers should check with local agencies, especially those heading for the Annapurna and Manaslu regions. Several passes there were already cut or in poor condition after the previous storm and subsequent floods.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Climbing teams

A Russian team in the Kangchenjunga region is acclimatizing to climb 7,710m Jannu. According to their latest report, they plan to touch 7,000m before attempting their main goal.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Fellow Russians attempting the West Ridge of Everest have retreated to Kathmandu to rest and recover, so they should not be affected. Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov, all climbing without supplemental oxygen, are enduring some lung problems. They returned to Base Camp from their second foray up the mountain last Friday, without reaching 7,500m, as they’d hoped.

Winter soloist replanning

After climbing in the Cholu range, Jost Kobusch of Germany and his small team moved to the Manaslu area for the second stage of his acclimatization before attempting Everest solo in winter, also without oxygen and via the West Ridge. However, the poor state of the trails after the recent floods and the approaching cyclone have thwarted his plans.

“The flood cut our planned path and, according to forecasts, the incoming cyclone will leave up to two meters of snow,” Kobusch told ExplorersWeb from Samagaon, where the team is pondering their options.

title: Climbers Find New Alpine Lines on Remote Peaks in Nepal - Gripped Climbing Magazine
description: Climbers Find New Alpine Lines on Remote Peaks in Nepal  Gripped Climbing Magazine
publisher.title: Gripped Climbing Magazine
full_article:
Swedish mountaineer Fredrik Sträng and Norwegian climber Sindre Kolbjørnsgard have claimed three first ascents in the remote Humla region of northwestern Nepal, including a technical mixed route graded up to M6 on a spectacular 5,337-metre peak. The pair reached the summit on October 18, 2026, after an expedition nearly derailed by heavy snowfall.

Gripped has been following Sträng’s expedition in recent weeks, the climbs offer a glimpse of a different kind of Himalayan mountaineering that seeks new routes and extends the possibilities for climbers in remote regions, without the extreme altitudes and commercial pressures associated with the world’s highest peaks.

The team’s original objective was an unclimbed mountain in the Nyalu Himal, but a snowstorm beginning September 24 dumped an estimated two metres of snow in parts of the region, making the approach across Nyalu La pass impractical. Rather than abandon the expedition, the climbers turned their attention to previously undocumented peaks accessible from their base camp near Phendol Kermi.

The standout objective was a striking, tooth-shaped summit the pair have provisionally named Daara Peak. Its north face offered a five-pitch technical line through loose rock, steep granite and a snow-filled couloir, followed by an exposed ridge leading to an eight-metre rock pinnacle at the summit. Their first attempt ended in retreat as snowfall worsened, but a clear weather window allowed them to return and complete the climb.

title: Bay of Bengal cyclone to bring rain to Nepal from Thursday - The Rising Nepal
description: Bay of Bengal cyclone to bring rain to Nepal from Thursday  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter, Kathmandu, Oct. 27: A cyclone developing in the Bay of Bengal is likely to bring rainfall to several parts of the country from Thursday, with some places expected to receive heavy rain.

The weather system is also expected to affect Kathmandu Valley, while farmers have been advised to harvest and bring in their paddy crops by Wednesday afternoon.

According to Rojan Lamichhane, a meteorologist at the Meteorological Forecasting Division under the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (DHM), the cyclone named Arnab is intensifying and is expected to develop into a severe cyclonic storm before making landfall near Yanam, between Andhra Pradesh and Visakhapatnam in India, on October 28.

The system is expected to gradually weaken as it moves inland towards Nepal, but it is likely to affect the country's Himalayan and hilly regions, with a greater impact expected in the Himalayas, Lamichhane said.

From Friday to Saturday, moderate rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms, lightning and strong winds is likely at many places in Koshi, Madhes, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces. A few places in these provinces may receive heavy rainfall.

Some places in Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces are also likely to receive moderate rainfall, with heavy rainfall possible at a few locations. According to a special post-monsoon bulletin issued by the DHM on Monday, rainfall may begin on Thursday and continue through Friday and Saturday. Cloud cover is expected to increase from Wednesday.

The bulletin said that while major river basins nationwide are expected to remain at normal levels on Wednesday, rainfall activity will cause water levels to begin rising by Thursday across the Narayani, Koshi, Bagmati, and Kamala basins.

Between Friday and Saturday, continuous heavy rainfall is projected to push river flows to their peak levels -- approaching warning and vigilance thresholds -- particularly in the Narayani, Koshi, Bagmati, Kamala, and Tinau basins, alongside minor surges in the Mahakali, Karnali, West Rapti, and Babai rivers.

The DHM also highlighted that the primary hazards during this storm event are concentrated in the hilly, Chure and Terai catchments, where small rivers and tributaries face high risks of flash floods and waterlogging.

Farmers have been advised to complete agricultural activities, including harvesting and bringing in paddy crops, before Thursday, as moderate rainfall is expected across many parts of the hills and Tarai, with heavy rainfall possible in a few places.

The DHM has also urged people to remain alert in the high hills and Himalayan regions, where heavy snowfall, snowstorms and avalanches are possible. Tourists have been advised against travelling to high Himalayan areas, while those already there have been urged to stay in safe places.

The weather system may also bring colder conditions, trigger landslides in vulnerable areas and along roads, and disrupt road and air transport as well as daily life. The public and concerned agencies have been urged to take necessary precautions and make preparations in advance.

The system’s influence is expected to gradually weaken from Saturday night, Lamichhane said.

title: Goat trade worth Rs. 40M in Humla during Dashain - The Rising Nepal
description: Goat trade worth Rs. 40M in Humla during Dashain  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By Our Correspondent, Humla/Nepalgunj, Oct. 27: Goats worth around Rs. 40 million were traded in the Himalayan district of Humla during Dashain this year, driven by the festival’s religious and cultural traditions, which include animal sacrifice.

Goat trader Man Bahadur Parki, who brought 400 goats from Saipal in Bajhang, said he had conducted business worth nearly Rs. 10 million. Although around 25 per cent of his sales were made on credit, he said this was the highest volume of Dashain trade he had done so far.

He said he had also brought goats for sale from Lipulek, Darchula and the Api Himal region in Sudurpaschim Province.

Another trader, Paldan Sunar, who sold around 350 goats, said he had also recorded his highest-ever sales during Dashain this year.

According to Sunar, local people bought goats priced between Rs. 20,000 and Rs. 35,000 for the festival’s sacrificial rituals. He attributed the increased sales of locally raised goats partly to China’s refusal to allow the import of chyangra (Himalayan mountain goats) through the Hilsa border crossing.

Local resident Jaya Bahadur Shahi, who purchased a goat for Rs. 34,000 for sacrifice during Dashain, said higher prices had not dampened demand.

Although traders had expected goat sales to decline compared with previous years, business had increased instead, he said, adding that the trade also reflected the cultural significance of Dashain.

For the first time, traders also transported four truckloads of goats from Humla to Pokhara for sale, extending the market beyond the district.

The Humla Chamber of Commerce and Industry also reported an increase in goat trading during Dashain. It said the trade had typically reached around Rs. 30 million during the festival in previous years, but sales were significantly higher this year.

Similarly, our Nepalgunj correspondent Siraj Khan adds, women farmers in Fattepur, Rapti Sonari Rural Municipality-6 of Banke district, sold 700 goats during this year’s Dashain festival, helping them cover their festival expenses.

Around 400 women farmers in the village have been raising goats commercially through the Naya Shrijanshil Social Entrepreneur Women’s Cooperative, according to its chairperson, Ganga Shah.

She said traders and consumers directly visited the cooperative during Dashain to purchase live goats, which were weighed and sold at Rs. 700 per kilogram. The sales enabled the women farmers to manage their expenses for the festival.

“The women bring the goats they have raised to the cooperative for sale. They have them weighed, and we sell the goats in their presence,” Shah said. “A total of 700 goats were sold during this year’s Dashain.”

Women engaged in commercial goat farming through the cooperative have contributed to increased goat production in Banke, Shah said. She added that women involved in goat farming were now selling between 10 and 12 goats a year. The cooperative has also helped women avoid the hassle of finding markets and the risk of being cheated by traders by managing the sale of goats raised by its members.

Sabitri Chaudhary, a woman farmer from Fattepur, said the cooperative’s direct involvement in selling goats had freed farmers from the difficulties of searching for buyers and being cheated by traders.

title: Reforming Universities - The Rising Nepal
description: Reforming Universities  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Following the opening up in the early 1990s, Nepal's higher education sector underwent significant change. The number of colleges and universities increased dramatically. Colleges run by the private sector also grew by leaps and bounds. Students got the opportunity to study new academic curricula and programmes. Though there has been diversification and specialisation of subjects, the Nepali universities were unable to satisfy the academic needs and passion of students. One visible problem facing our universities is the absence of specialised programmes that link education with innovation, entrepreneurship and the job market. An outdated curriculum, a focus on theoretical teaching and learning, political interference, frequent student agitations, and politically motivated teacher and student unions discourage many students from enrolling in the country's top academic institutions. This is a reason why Nepali students are leaving the country en masse daily.





Nepali universities must impart quality education to students in line with global standards in order to check brain drain and enhance the nation’s intellectual profile. Realising the need for monitoring the quality of universities, the Nepal government established the University Grants Commission (UGC) in 1993 as an autonomous statutory body. Its goals include promoting and facilitating the universities for quality higher education, enabling educational institutions to fulfil the national need for an educated and trained workforce and sorting out challenges that have hindered the development and quality of higher education, among others. It is struggling to monitor the growing number of universities and foster innovative ideas and knowledge. In May this year, the UGC unveiled a national academic calendar to enhance the efficiency of academic activities in higher education institutions as part of the university reform plan.





However, the UGC is itself in need of sweeping reforms in today's changing landscape of the education sector. Without revamping itself, it is unlikely to promote educational standards in higher education. Newly appointed UGC chairman Dr. Khadga KC, while talking to this daily, has stressed amending its legal framework to pursue the much-desired university reforms. Dr. KC and his team are determined to amend the UGC Act enacted in 1994. It should have a fresh structural and conceptual framework. Initiatives have been taken to gather the views of stakeholders to form a comprehensive view of the UGC’s legal provisions. Revising the new law is a prerequisite for the reforms in higher education in line with the evolving dynamics in the sector. Currently, altogether 20 universities are operating at the federal and provincial level. However, there is no proper study and research on how many universities Nepal needs to provide quality education for students. Increasing universities only ramps up costs. So the UGC should conduct research to determine the number of universities we need.





Nepali varsities have limited resources that hinder them from conducting research and producing knowledge. Experts suggest setting up specialised schools like MIT and IIT instead of adding new universities. Universities require connecting research to local communities and industrial growth so that opportunities will be available for the bulge of youth. Achieving financial autonomy should be the first priority of the UGC. It is largely dependent on donor agencies. Currently, around 70 per cent of the total higher education budget allocated by the UGC goes to the TU. Without adequate investment in research and development, universities can't attract students and meet their intellectual needs. The UGC must not confine its role to monitoring universities but it should also impel them to attain academic excellence.

title: Nepal approves drafting law on agency for Budhigandaki HPP — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal approves drafting law on agency for Budhigandaki HPP — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, the Cabinet of Ministers on October 16 approved in principle the drafting of a bill to establish the Budhigandaki Development Agency for the 1,200 MW hydropower project. The decision once again calls into question the implementation model for the project, whose financial structure had previously been approved, Kathmandu Post reports.

Change in implementation model

In the budget for the current fiscal year, Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle announced that the hydropower plant would be developed through an authorized agency. In the previous year's budget, then Finance Minister Bishnu Paudel proposed a public-private partnership model. The project received national priority status in the 2012–2013 fiscal year and was planned to be completed by 2026–2027.

Former Energy Secretary Anup Upadhyay criticized the idea of creating a new body. He believes that government spending on the project should be counted as equity, while the remaining funds should be raised from investors. Officials at the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation also warned that drafting the law and establishing the agency could slow down the implementation of the hydropower project.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Financing and cost

The project's financial structure was approved by the interim government formed in September 2025. Under the plan, 70% of the cost is to be financed through debt and 30% through equity. The base cost of the hydropower plant on the border of Dhading and Gorkha districts is estimated at $2.77 billion, or about 374 billion rupees. Including 32 billion rupees in interest during construction, the total could reach 406 billion rupees.

Budhigandaki Jalbidyut Company Limited, which is advancing the project, has already begun preparing the draft law. Its head, Arun Rajauria, said that existing contracts and work would not be halted, and that after the agency is established, the company's responsibilities and activities would be transferred to the new structure. The government is to provide 97.47 billion rupees in equity and 150 billion rupees in concessional loans, while the Nepal Electricity Authority is to provide another 24.37 billion rupees in equity.

title: In Nepal, people return to flood-damaged homes — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: In Nepal, people return to flood-damaged homes — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, residents of the Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts affected by the Bhotekoshi flood on August 26 are returning to homes covered in silt and debris. People cannot afford to pay rent for long periods, while government assistance promised to many families has not yet arrived, and safety inspections of buildings remain incomplete, Kathmandu Post reports.

Devighat resident Ram Kumar Bhandari returned to his own house in Bidur-5 Municipality with his family of seven. After the flood, the family rented accommodation in Pipaltar for about a month but could not afford to rent an entire house. According to Bhandari, caring for his mother, who has a mental disorder, was also difficult in someone else’s home. He said that around 15 families from his area had also moved back into damaged homes: some live on upper floors, while others are clearing the silt themselves.

Assistance has not arrived

The Nepalese government decided to provide displaced families with monthly living assistance for six months or until alternative housing becomes available. Households of up to four people are to receive 15,000 Nepalese rupees per month, with an additional 2,000 rupees for each additional family member.

Rabindra Nepal, chair of Bidur-7 Ward and spokesperson for the municipality, said that no displaced family in the municipality had yet received the payments because the funds had not been transferred. Ram Bahadur KS, a representative of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said that local authorities are identifying, registering and verifying aid recipients.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

According to the authority, the government allocated 370 million rupees for assistance, of which 184.86 million rupees were distributed among 4,108 households identified by local authorities. Each received a first installment of 45,000 rupees. At the same time, the authority’s report does not specify how many families have already received monthly rent compensation.

Uncertain resettlement

Authorities say they will not allow settlements to be rebuilt in areas at high risk of flooding. At the same time, the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction has preliminarily surveyed 2,027 households, but the report does not include data on the number of houses that have undergone structural safety assessments.

As of October 16, 943 displaced people were staying at 13 temporary accommodation sites. In Rasuwa, residents of Timure inspected plots for collective resettlement, including in the settlement of Haku, where most families have ancestral land. According to KS, more than 3,000 land plots have been identified for temporary and transitional housing in Nuwakot and Rasuwa, but their suitability still needs to be assessed and legal procedures have not been completed.

title: Jazzmandu 2026 - Nepali Times
description: Jazzmandu 2026  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
The annual Surya Nepal Jazzmandu is returning to Nepal’s capital for its 22nd edition between two major festivals Dasain and Tihar between 29 October – 4 November.

Eleven musicians and bands will be performing, including musicians from the United States, Brazil, Switzerland, France, Australia, Singapore, and Nepal.

“Every year is unique but this year’s main attraction is that various musicians from around the world are coming together, especially Tito Puente Jr, son of Tito Puente, the pioneer of Latin jazz,” says Navin Chettri, founder of the festival and member of Cadenza Collective (see below).

Jazz Upstairs Bar’s Chhedup Bomzan and Cadenza’s drummer and singer Chettri started the concerts for the first time in 2002 and it has been held almost every year since.

“The seed of the festival was planted in Australia when we were invited to a Jazz festival over there,” recalls Chettri. “The whole idea was to bring the live jazz scene in Kathmandu, so that people can share the energy of musicians around the world.”

Tito Puente Jr, USA

Tito Puente Jr continues the legacy of his jazz legend father Tito Puente. In just five short years, he has already become an audience favourite and has performed in 300 concerts around the world.

Puente has been featured in several major American television networks, and his 2004 album In My Father’s Shoes was adapted into a BET Jazz television special. His latest album, Got Mambo?, features both traditional rhythms and audacious new approaches that establishes his own distinct jazz voice.

Tito Puente Jr – Timbale and vocals | Zach Fawcett – Trumpet | Pravin Chettri – Alto saxophone | Inap Raj Shretha – Tenor saxophone | Nick Aggs – Baritone saxophone | Manon Mullener – Piano | Samir Chettri – Bass | Navin Chettri – Percussion | Alex Brindell – Percussion | Philippe Ciminato – Percussion

Manon Mullener, Switzerland

Manon Mullener started playing piano at the age of four. At seventeen, her love of jazz, especially Afro-Cuban music, took her to Havana for creative training. Mullener has since toured and played widely in Europe, Latin America, and the West Asia. She is regarded as a rising talent of European jazz and was given the Swiss Jazz Award in 2026.

Her first album, Reflejos (2019) was recorded in collaboration with Peruvian pianist César Correa and Zurich-based percussionist David Stauffacher. Inspired by people she met during her tours, STORIES (2024) was recorded in New York, and it received praise from the European press.

She is an awardee of the Spirale Prize and got a top spot in the 2022 SOFIA (Support of Female Improvising Artists) international competition.

Manon Mullener – Piano | Lucien Mullener – Drums | Rodrigo Aravena – Bass

Cadenza Collective, Nepal

Cadenza Collective is one of the most distinctive and eclectic bands to come out from Kathmandu. It has revitalised Nepal’s improvised music scene, performed internationally, and collaborated with a diverse range of Western and traditional Nepali musicians.

“This festival gives us a chance for us band members to be together, as we all live in different countries,” says Chettri. “We are excited to share the energy and music as in all these 23 years,” says drummer and composer Navin Chettri

The band has released seven original albums, with its latest singles, The Mountain Tickled My Feet and Selo Groove, scheduled for release in 2026.

Navin Chettri – Vocals and drums | Rajat Rai – Guitar | Inap Raj Shrestha – Tenor Sax | Pravin Chhetri – Alto Sax | Samir Chettri – Bass | Zach Fawcett – Trumpet (guest artist)

Kanta dAb dAb, Nepal

Kanta dAb dAb combines sitar, bass, and percussion to fuse ethnic, traditional, Nepali classical, and various Western musical influences, resulting in a vibrant, soulful, cross-genre sound that remains distinctly Nepali and modern. They reinterpret Nepal’s traditional and folk music within a contemporary framework, believing that the country’s musical heritage inspires musicians and scholars alike. Kanta dAb dAb also co-founded Echoes In The Valley, Nepal’s only free folk and indigenous music festival.

The band is also inspired by the diverse experiences of its three members who have been leading figures in Nepal’s music scene for over twenty years. Riju Tuladhar, Sunit Kansakar, and Nikhil Tuladhar, each having mastered their respective instrument, are regarded as veteran musicians.

Nikhil Tuladhar – Drums | Sunit Kansakar – Sitar | Rizu Tuladhar – Bass

Cesar Haas, Brazil

Brazilian guitarist, composer, instructor, and director of the WSU Brazilian Jazz Fest, César Haas received his Doctor of Musical Arts from the Eastman School of Music and is currently an assistant professor of jazz and classical guitar at Washington State University. He has performed in Brazil and the United States with acclaimed artists including Ken Peplowski, Scotty Barnhart, Bobby Militello among others.

Haas’ works were featured on Nelson Faria’s renowned Um Café Lá em Casa series and he has recorded soundtrack for the documentary Doutor Araguaia. He has collaborated with trombonist Dave Glenn (from legendary Gerry Mulligan big band) presenting original music that blends Brazilian traditions with contemporary jazz.

Cesar Haas – Guitar | Pravin Chettri – Bass | Navin Chettri – Drums

Hot Club of Patan, Nepal

From Patan is a group of musicians who are inclined to music from the 1930s and 40s with jazz stylings of the duo Stephane Grappelli and Django Reinhardt. The band incorporates a multitude of rhythmical styles including swing, bossa and valse, improvising their tunes.

In addition, the band also interprets classic Nepali pop songs from Narayan Gopal and other musical legends from the 60s and 70s and puts in their own spin, gaining them popularity among the Nepali audience.

Chakra – Guitar | Rigzin – Guitar | Sovan – Guitar | Kunzanne – Vocal | Riken – Double bass

Kevin Saura Group, France

Kevin Saura is a French guitarist and composer based in Nice. Before studying at CNRR with Philippe Petit, Fréderic Luzignant, Jean-Paul Ceccareli, and Robert Persi, he taught himself music at the tender age of eight. He later formed Shaky Things as a trio in 2016 and toured multiple countries around the world including France, Italy, Spain, Belgium among others.

The Kevin Saura Group’s philosophy combines jazz lineage with contemporary funk grooves, free jazz freedom, blues-rock hues, and melodic lines from West Coast jazz and bebop. Their music exhibits maturity in the composition of the pieces while maintaining the vibrant intensity of live performance. Each instrument finds its place owing to the core group’s passionate close-knit musicians.

Kevin Saura – Guitar | Roman Dauneau – Bass | Félix Joveniaux – Drums | Philippe Ciminato – Percussion

Nick Aggs Quartet, Australia

Nick Aggs collaborated with Australian fusion band Afro Dizzi Act for his debut performance in Kathmandu in 2002. This year, he is returning for the 8th time with a new quartet. Aggs successfully built his career as a performer, composer and a bandleader with performances at various festivals throughout Asia, Middle East and Australia.

Ant Aggs, his brother and a fellow founding member of Afro Dizzi Act, Mike Hicks, Nick’s long-time musical partner from his years in Shanghai, and Alex Brindell, a Singapore-based drummer and regular collaborator is joining him for this edition. The quartet’s music spans from deep grooves, lyrical improvisation that blends contemporary jazz, funk and global influences.

Nick Aggs – Saxophone | Ant Aggs – Keys | Alex Brindell – Drums | Mike Hicks – Bass

Eastern Classical Musicians, Nepal

Eastern Classical Musicians is made up of musicians like Jonisha Poudel, an accomplished exponent of khayal. Poudel is pursuing her PhD at Rabindra Bharati University in Kolkata, studying khayal and thumri under Maestro Debapriya Adhikary. She is an awardee of the Yuva Pratibha Samman in 2019 and has sung for Nepali films as well. She has also performed in different platforms along with a solo concert at the National Cultural Academy.

Santosh Bhakta Shrestha has dedicated himself to the ishraj for two and a half decades. A pupil of Mohan Joshi, Shrestha has mastered the instrument, and performed in many countries and contributed to multiple recordings.

Having collaborated with national and international artists, Roshan Putwar is a musician and researcher of Eastern classical and Nepali traditional music. Putwar represented Nepal at the South Asian Residency 2017 and has performed in more than a thousand stages across multiple countries.

Jonisha Poudel–Vocals | Santosh Bhakt–Ishraj | Roshan Putwar–Bamboo flute

Milan & Milesh Duo, Nepal

Milan Tandukar got his Master’s degree from Pragya Sangeet Samithi in Allahabad with the likes of Mohan Prasad Joshi, Pandit Kumar Lal Shrestha and Pandit Prem Chandra Ojhaya adding to his knowledge of the violin. He has worked as an artist in Radio Nepal and Nepal Television, and is the winner of multiple awards including Kalanidhi Music Award (Gold Metal).

Milesh Tandukar is the founder president of Pundit Satya Narayan Chaudhary Memorial Academy and has a master’s degree in tabala from Prayag Sangeet Samiti in Allahabad. A versatile musician, he can play a wide range of instruments including Dhime, Khin, Nagada, Bango, Dhol among others. He has toured around the globe and worked in albums Musical Journey to Shindhuli Gadhi & Voiceles voice and Trinetra.

Gandharva, Nepal

Historically, the Gandharva troubadours are regarded as the link between heaven and earth, minstrels who mediate between mortals and the gods. They used to earn a living by playing music traveling from village to village. The lyrics carried news of current affairs to the public before radio, television and the internet. They were also known as Walking Newspapers.

title: Mobilise Remittances For Growth - The Rising Nepal
description: Mobilise Remittances For Growth  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Recent data show that remittance inflows in Nepal have increased substantially. Remittances are the money sent by our migrant workers to their families. With our increasing labour dependency, remittances have become a major source of household income, foreign exchange reserves, and several other developmental outcomes. In the last fiscal year alone, Nepal received Rs. 2.36 trillion in remittances. This is 35.8 per cent of the size of our GDP and a 37 per cent increase from the previous year. In the first two months of this fiscal year (Shrawan and Bhadra 2083) alone, Rs 436.36 billion has been received. Data reveal that during the 1993-2024 period, remittance inflow grew by nearly 19 per cent per year. It has exceeded the annual national budget. In this context, it is worthwhile to understand the causes and consequences of the growth in remittance inflows.

There are internal, external and institutional causes of rising remittance inflows. As Nepal’s economy could not expand significantly in the last four decades, unemployment and underemployment persisted. Limited availability of well-paid jobs at home forced our youth to seek work abroad, where wage earnings have been much higher than here. Nepal’s limited industrialisation due to cheap imports exported our jobs abroad. Many families also could not meet their family's financial needs. This forced them to migrate for work. Seeing that many families have improved their living standards from remittances, others have naturally been attracted to foreign employment. The number of Nepalis flying for foreign employment has also increased steadily since 1990. Many have gone repeatedly means they benefited from it.

Facilitation

The government has also facilitated migration for work with the required laws and other support measures. With the increase in migrant workers due to various domestic push factors, remittance inflows also increased. Some external factors have also caused increased remittance inflows. Construction, hospitality, manufacturing, care services and other sectors have seen huge expansion in the Golf and Malaysia. This increased demand for foreign labour in these destinations. Many of our migrant workers also benefitted from their migration networks, as some of their earlier known migrants helped to pull their relatives and friends.

There was also diversification of destinations. Precisely, employment opportunities in Gulf countries, Malaysia, Japan, South Korea, Europe and other high-wage destinations broaden income sources for our migrant workers. It is the family obligations of our migrant workers who regularly send money to support their relatives back home. The continuous depreciation of the Nepali rupee against most of the foreign currencies has also posted increased remittance inflows. The combination of these external factors accelerated Nepal’s dependency on foreign jobs and remittances.

Some institutional factors have also played very crucial role in increased remittance incomes. With the availability of formal banking and technology-enabled digital transfer systems, remittance transfers have become less costly and safe. This made money movement quicker and easily recorded, unlike the informal Hundi system. The emergence of foreign employment-related institutions such as the foreign employment department with its authority to carry out labour approvals, the foreign employment board for dealing with a host of foreign employment-related problems, private recruitment agencies for supplying migrant workers and bilateral labour mechanisms for securing the rights of these workers has also helped remittance growth.

Like any income, increased remittance inflows have both positive and negative consequences. Their overall impact depends on how households, financial institutions and the government use this income. On the positive side, when remittance inflows increase, such household income helps families meet basic needs and withstand economic shocks. Evidence shows that this has helped reduce poverty. Also, despite some families being badly affected, remittance inflows have improved the living standards of several migrant households. Their access to education, healthcare, housing, sanitation and nutrition facilities has broadened. This has certainly helped improve human development in the country.

Besides, remittances have helped finance imports and strengthen external-sector stability. It has also helped offset part of Nepal's persistent merchandise trade deficit. Since households accumulate savings and access financial services, it has helped realise the financial inclusion targets of the government. Many returnee migrant workers have also become entrepreneurs of farms and small businesses. Increased remittance inflows have also some negative consequences. As households tend to spend more on imported vehicles, electronics, fuel and consumer goods, remittances have increased import demand and thereby growing trade deficits.

Evidence shows that remittances have mostly been spent on unproductive sectors, such as consumption and real estate. This has not expanded enterprises and employment opportunities. Outmigration has reduced domestic labour supply. The increase in uncultivated land due to labour shortages across the country is a good illustration here. Moreover, it has also been argued that increased remittance inflows have contributed to real exchange-rate pressures amidst productivity stagnation. Excessive dependence upon remittances has also exposed households and the national economy to economic and other shocks abroad. Non-migrant households are likely to earn less income and thereby inequality may grow in our society.

Social consequences

We have also observed some social consequences of remittance inflows. Family separation and emotional stress for migrants and their dependents have multiplied. Caregiving burdens on spouses, grandparents and other family members have also increased. Children of migrant workers have lost their rights to grow with their parents. There are several cases of exploitation, unsafe working conditions abroad, recruitment fraud and excessive migration-related debt for some households. The domestic labour market has been losing skilled and experienced workers.

Understanding the above-stated causes and consequences of booming remittance inflows inspires some policy implications. There is a clear need to reduce long-term remittance-dependency by mobilising remittances in various employment generating sectors. A conducive policy environment must be created for investment and priority must be accorded to human capital development. Equally, we need to transform migration governance, reduce excessive imports and target high-wage destinations.





(Dr. Bhusal writes on various developmental issues.)

title: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News - Khabarhub
description: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Economic Digest presents a brief yet comprehensive roundup of major business developments in Nepal, delivered in clear and accessible summaries.

Nepal’s post-Dashain economic landscape reflects mixed financial performance, ongoing governance challenges, and emerging opportunities for development. The NEPSE index declined by 4.34 points to 2,629, ending a seven-session rally, while transaction turnover reached Rs 4 billion. Conversely, gold and silver prices rebounded, indicating renewed movement in the domestic precious metals market. Neoteric Nepal’s 40 percent turnover growth and Global IME Bank’s third consecutive international banking award demonstrate private-sector expansion and strengthening institutional recognition.

Governance and public administration remain significant concerns. The Nepal Oil Corporation’s renewed VAT billing directive highlights efforts to improve tax compliance, while substantial relief fund balances indicate considerable resources for disaster response. However, staff shortages in Bagmati’s cooperative management committee threaten timely recovery of depositors’ savings, despite government assurances of accelerated repayments. Sudurpashchim’s administrative expenditure also raises questions about balancing operational costs with development priorities.

Infrastructure and regional development initiatives offer opportunities for economic progress. Road expansion, proposed improvements to Karnali’s air connectivity, and agricultural commercialization could enhance mobility, employment, and rural incomes. Nevertheless, declining millet cultivation reveals weaknesses in traditional agricultural support systems. Women’s marigold farming in Tanahu demonstrates how collective entrepreneurship can strengthen local markets and financial independence.

Overall, Nepal’s economic outlook presents both resilience and structural vulnerabilities. Effective implementation, institutional accountability, agricultural support, and inclusive development policies will be essential for sustainable growth.

NEPSE drops 4.34 points after Dashain as turnover reaches Rs 4 billion

The Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) index declined by 4.34 points to close at 2,629 on Monday, the first trading day after the Dashain holiday. The decline ended its seven-session upward trend. Share prices of 99 companies increased, while 171 declined and six remained unchanged. Total transaction turnover reached Rs 4 billion, down from Rs 4.88 billion in the previous trading session. The Manufacturing and Processing group rose by 1.03 percent, while the Trading group gained 1.11 percent. Higher share prices of cement companies supported the manufacturing sector, while a 1.41 percent increase in Bishal Bazar Company contributed to gains in the trading group. Newly listed Beni Hydropower posted the highest gain of the session, rising 15 percent. Chirkhwa Hydropower recorded the largest decline, with its share price falling 7.92 percent.

Gold rises to Rs 281,500 per tola, silver reaches Rs 3,995

The price of gold in Nepal’s domestic market increased by Rs 3,000 per tola on Monday, October 26, reaching Rs 281,500 after trading resumed following the Dashain festival. Gold had previously declined by Rs 11,700 per tola to Rs 278,500. Silver prices also increased, rising by Rs 40 per tola to Rs 3,995, according to the Federation of Nepal Gold and Silver Dealers’ Association. On the previous trading day, silver had fallen by Rs 195 to Rs 3,955 per tola. One tola is equivalent to approximately 11.66 grams.

NOC directs LPG industries to issue VAT bills on all sales

The Nepal Oil Corporation has instructed all liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) industries and bottling plants to issue value-added tax (VAT) bills for every sale, following reports of widespread non-compliance across regional distribution networks. In a formal circular signed by Director Engineer Binit Mani Upadhyay, the corporation reiterated its earlier directives issued on August 14, 2024, and January 23, 2025. The instructions require designated regional dealers and commercial distributors to provide official tax invoices for all retail transactions to promote transparency and ensure compliance with tax regulations in the energy sector.

Relief funds for prime minister collect more than Rs 18 billion

Contributions to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund and the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund have continued following floods in the Bhote Koshi River in Rasuwa. According to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, the combined balance of the funds stood at Rs 18.09 billion as of 9 am on the day of the report. Of the total, Rs 13.48 billion is held in various accounts at nine commercial banks under the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund. The funds also hold USD 3.04 million in accounts at Himalayan Bank and Laxmi Sunrise Bank. The government has been collecting financial contributions through these funds to support rescue and relief operations in flood-affected areas.

Officials discuss challenges facing air services in Karnali Province

Government representatives and private airline operators held discussions on Monday about difficulties affecting air services in Karnali Province and potential measures to improve connectivity. The meeting was attended by Minister for Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Khadak Raj Paudel, also known as Ganesh; the Karnali Province Minister for Industry, Tourism, Forest and Environment; officials from the provincial ministry; the director general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CAAN); and private airline operators serving the province’s mountainous districts. Participants discussed operational difficulties associated with providing flights across Karnali’s challenging terrain and explored ways to improve air services in the region. However, the official statement did not specify the particular challenges raised or detail the measures proposed during the discussions.

Minister Rawal discusses cooperative victims’ concerns during Chitwan visit

Minister for Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration Pratibha Rawal met victims of troubled cooperatives in Chitwan on Monday to hear their concerns and provide updates on government efforts to address their problems. Speaking to journalists at Bharatpur Airport, Rawal said resolving the difficulties faced by landless citizens and cooperative victims remained a government priority. She stated that the process of returning savings to depositors affected by distressed cooperatives had begun and would be accelerated. According to Rawal, the government has introduced policy changes to address legal barriers to refunding cooperative deposits and issuing landownership certificates to people who have occupied land for an extended period. She also sought to reassure people concerned about possible eviction, saying the government was working to settle outstanding issues. Rawal added that ministers should visit communities to listen to people’s concerns and explain government initiatives rather than expect citizens to approach them.

Staff shortages hamper Bagmati’s troubled cooperative management committee

The Problematic Cooperative Management Committee, established by the Bagmati Provincial Government in fiscal year 2023/24 to oversee distressed financial institutions, is facing operational delays because of a shortage of personnel. The committee has only 12 staff members against an approved quota of 24 positions. It has also operated without a chartered accountant for three consecutive years. The committee oversees five troubled savings and credit cooperatives: Civil, Sumeru, Lalitpur-based Lali Gurans, Darshan and National Namobuddha. Partial refunds have been distributed to small depositors at two of the cooperatives. Depositors with savings of less than Rs 100,000 at National Namobuddha and those with less than Rs 50,000 at Sumeru have received partial repayments.

Sudurpashchim allocates more than Rs 3.04 billion for salaries and administrative expenses

The Sudurpashchim Provincial Government has allocated more than Rs 3.04 billion in its approved budget for fiscal year 2026/27 to cover salaries, allowances, uniforms, food, medical expenses and awards for elected representatives and government employees. The allocation includes Rs 2.85 billion from provincial internal revenue and Rs 198.5 million from federal grants. An additional Rs 4.9 million has been earmarked for staff social security. The provincial government has also set aside Rs 31.9 million for fuel, vehicle maintenance, insurance and equipment servicing. Of this amount, Rs 11.9 million is specifically allocated for fuel expenses at government offices across the province.

Millet cultivation declines in Jumla despite flour selling at Rs 200 per kg

Millet cultivation is declining in Jumla despite growing market demand for finger millet flour, which sells for Rs 200 per kilogram. Farmers are increasingly moving away from traditional crops because of limited commercial production opportunities and inadequate promotional support. According to the Agriculture Development Office, Jumla produced 3,850 metric tons of millet across 2,740 hectares in the previous fiscal year. The crop was cultivated across all eight local government units in the district. Traditional crops are losing ground as younger generations increasingly turn to vegetable farming and other cash crops. Agricultural experts say institutional support for production, processing and marketing could help preserve indigenous crops while improving farmers’ incomes.

Road expansion project identifies 219 structures encroaching on right-of-way

The Department of Roads under the Ministry of Infrastructure Development has finalized a revised resettlement action plan for the Kamaladi-Dhalkebar-Bagmati section of the Asian Highway-2, which is being expanded with support from the World Bank. The 77-kilometre road section passes through Dhanusha, Mahottari and Sarlahi districts. The project aims to upgrade the existing two-lane road to at least four lanes, with expansion to six lanes in urban commercial areas. The project is targeted for completion by mid-2027. Field inspections conducted between January and October 2025 identified 219 structures encroaching on the road corridor. According to the revised plan, all the structures lie within the designated 50-metre right-of-way established through a gazette notification in 1977. As a result, the project does not require the acquisition of additional private land.

Women in Aandhimul target Rs 1 million in marigold sales during Tihar

A group of 45 women engaged in commercial flower farming in Aandhimul, Aabukhaireni Rural Municipality-1, Tanahu, aims to generate Rs 1 million from marigold sales during the upcoming Tihar festival. The group has expanded its cultivation area to 45 ropanis after earning Rs 900,000 from flower sales last year. Harvesting, storage and distribution preparations are underway, with harvested marigolds being kept in cold storage to maintain their freshness before reaching the market. The flowers are expected to sell for up to Rs 400 per kilogram. Gift shop operators in Damauli have already purchased an initial shipment of 50 kilograms. The initiative has increased local flower production, reduced dependence on supplies from outside the region and created additional income opportunities for women involved in the farming group.

London-based Nepalis donate Rs 10 million and DNA testing kits to government

Two non-resident Nepalis based in London have contributed Rs 10 million and DNA testing kits to the government to strengthen its research and DNA testing capabilities. Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal received a cheque worth Rs 10 million from Uttam Nepal and DNA testing kits from Kul Acharya during an event at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday. Khanal expressed gratitude to both donors, saying their contributions would help enhance the government’s capacity for research and DNA testing. The event was attended by House of Representatives member Vidushi Rana, representatives of the Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) and senior officials from the ministry.

Neoteric Nepal posts record annual turnover of nearly Rs 4.87 billion

Neoteric Nepal, a company under the Golchha Group, recorded a turnover of Rs 4.869 billion in the last fiscal year, marking a 40 percent increase from the previous year. The company reported turnover of Rs 3.491 billion in 2025 and Rs 3.66 billion in 2024. Strong demand for Dell computing equipment, Haier home appliances and Nokia telecommunications products contributed to its growth. Neoteric Nepal recorded a net profit margin of 1.68 percent, while its gross cash accrual rose to Rs 99 million. The company represents more than 30 international technology brands through five showrooms across the country. It also secured credit facilities carrying a combined rating of Rs 3.794 billion, comprising Rs 619.7 million in long-term facilities and Rs 3.175 billion in short-term credit lines to support its technology import business.

Global IME Bank receives Global Finance’s Best Bank Award for third consecutive year

Global IME Bank Limited has received the Best Bank Award 2026 from international financial publication Global Finance, marking the third consecutive year it has earned the recognition following awards in 2024 and 2025. The award was presented at a ceremony in Bangkok, Thailand. The recognition highlights the bank’s ability to mobilize financial resources, institutional credibility, expansion of digital services and geographical reach, strategic partnerships, customer-focused innovation, use of artificial intelligence, sustainable lending and risk management practices. Global IME Bank is the first commercial bank in Nepal to receive the award. Its nationwide network comprises 341 branches, 366 ATMs, 147 branchless banking units, 69 extension counters and three foreign representative offices, with operations covering all 77 districts.

Agriculture Development Bank restores digital banking services after security upgrades

Agriculture Development Bank has announced the resumption of its core digital banking services following temporary precautionary suspensions introduced in response to global cybersecurity concerns involving web-based PSP2 shell security protocols. Bank representatives said online infrastructure running on upgraded PHP software versions was not affected by the potential vulnerabilities. They added that technical security audits had been completed across all database servers. Internet banking, mobile banking and other transaction services are now fully operational. However, online account-opening services remain temporarily unavailable as the bank upgrades the relevant software. The service is expected to return in an improved format in the near future.

Vision Lumbini Energy schedules AGM to approve 3.6842 percent cash dividend

Vision Lumbini Energy Company has scheduled its annual general meeting (AGM) for Thursday, November 19, at Diyalo Foodland in Kalinagar, Butwal. The meeting is set to begin at 9 am. Shareholders will discuss the company’s annual performance and financial statements, appoint statutory auditors and consider approval of a cash dividend of 3.6842 percent of the paid-up capital, inclusive of applicable taxes. The company has also announced a book-closure date of December 2 to determine shareholders eligible for voting and dividend benefits. According to the notice, shareholders recorded on the Nepal Stock Exchange through Mangsir 13 will be eligible to participate in the meeting.

Pakistani players’ participation in NPL remains uncertain over reported PCB fee demand

The participation of Pakistani cricketers in the upcoming Nepal Premier League (NPL) remains uncertain after tournament stakeholders were reportedly instructed to temporarily halt players’ travel until the required no-objection certificates (NOCs) are issued. According to reports, the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) has allegedly sought around USD 25,000 for each player’s NOC. However, the reported fee demand has not been formally confirmed in writing. The uncertainty has prompted the affected players to adjust their travel plans. The tournament, featuring eight franchises, is scheduled to run from Monday through November 21. The Pakistani players expected to participate include Sahibzada Farhan, Haider Ali, Hunain Shah, Hussain Talat, Iftikhar Ahmed, Hasan Ali and Usama Mir. None of the listed players is currently part of an active Pakistan Test or One-Day International squad.

BY A STAFF REPORTER, Kathmandu, Oct. 27: Jeevan Ram Shrestha, President of the Nepal Olympic Committee (NOC), has bid farewell to the Nepali contingent heading to the Dakar Youth Olympic Games, which will be held in Dakar, Senegal, from October 31 to November 13, 2026.

During the farewell ceremony held at the NOC building in Satdobato, President Shrestha congratulated the athletes on securing the opportunity to participate in an international competition and urged them to make the most of this experience.

He encouraged them to demonstrate discipline, dedication and sportsmanship, and to strive for an outstanding performance that would bring pride to the nation.

The event, hosted by NOC General Secretary Rajiv Shrestha, was attended by the athletes, coaches, and officials who will represent Nepal at the Dakar Youth Olympic Games. Nepal will compete in three sports: swimming, Wushu and judo.

The Nepali contingent includes swimming coach Shankar Karki, along with athletes Aviv Pradhan and Arya Maharjan. Additionally, Wushu coach Lanam Lama and athlete Rashmi Tamang, as well as judoka Shubhanan Timilsina, will participate in the games.

Serving as team officials are NOC Deputy General Secretary Ramji Bahadur Hona Shrestha and NOC Secretary Bhim Singh Gurung.

The Nepal Olympic Committee has extended its best wishes for a successful participation, expressing confidence that the athletes representing Nepal on this international stage will deliver an excellent performance and gain valuable experience.

publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By Tilachan Pandey, Gulmi (Tamghas), Oct. 27: A unique three-way suspension bridge, considered a model project in the country, has yet to be formally handed over due to an internal dispute among the construction contractors.

Although the bridge took nearly 10 years to complete, it has remained unhanded over for four years. Construction of the bridge, which was inaugurated on December 1, 2014, was completed four years ago. The bridge is currently in use, but it has not been officially handed over to the concerned government office.

New Bato, Rubina and Mana Joint Venture (JV) was awarded the contract to build the suspension bridge across the Kali Gandaki River at Ridi, where Gulmi, Syangja and Palpa districts meet. The bridge connects the three districts.

On June 25, 2014, the joint venture signed an agreement with the Suspension Bridge Division under the Department of Local Infrastructure Development and Agricultural Roads (DoLIDAR), Pulchowk, to complete the project within three years at a cost of Rs. 98.82 million.

The Suspension Bridge Division Office in Kathmandu said the deadline was extended three times before construction was completed.

Construction contractor Mahendra Adhikari said the bridge could not be handed over because a subcontractor had filed a case, claiming that it had not been paid.

He said the main contractor had been unable to pay the subcontractor because the government office had not released the outstanding payments. He added that efforts were underway to settle the dispute.

With around 40 per cent of the payment involved, there were few other options available to resolve the matter, he said.

Shankar Budhathoki, planning chief at the office, said the handover process had been halted because of the contractors' internal dispute and a case pending at the Kaski District Court. The office said around 40 per cent of the project payment remained outstanding because of the dispute. The handover process will remain suspended until the contractors resolve their differences, Budhathoki said.

The office said coordination among the local governments of all three districts was necessary to ensure the bridge's long-term operation and maintenance. It is working with the three local governments to establish a sustainable management arrangement.
